/ section 1 · digital evidence

Evidence of Work

Three artefacts spanning data validation, reporting infrastructure, and recurring portfolio operations.

Artefact 01 Data Reconciliation & Business Logic Validation

Description

A data validation workstream spanning two related pieces of work. Datalake validation checks that data flowing from eFront and DealCloud into the Databricks data lake is processed correctly: waterfall logic, field mappings, and transformation rules are all verified against a source-to-target mapping document and a Data Quality Rules table. eFront UAT compares outputs from the Front Cube server against the existing eFront calculation engine to confirm values match within acceptable tolerance before Front Cube is adopted as the primary reporting server.

The wider Datalake project was initiated because key operational data sits across Capital IQ, eFront, and DealCloud, making manual extraction and reporting time-consuming and repetitive. My validation focus was on the Dimension and Mapping tables after raw tables were loaded, including extract timestamps, audit table entries, generated primary keys, transformation rules, and data quality checks that populate error or reprocess tables when new records violate expected logic.

My Contribution

For the Datalake validation, I reviewed source-to-target mapping documents to understand how eFront and DealCloud data was combined and transformed, including the waterfall logic that determines which source to use when both systems reference the same field. I performed column-level reconciliation between the Raw and Computed Layers in Databricks, flagged cases where the mapping document itself was incorrect, and built reusable PySpark validation utilities covering comparison logic, deduplication, metric verification, and automated Excel export, so that validation runs could be repeated consistently across tables. For the eFront UAT, I ran side-by-side comparisons between Front Cube and the original engine across multiple funds, checking that cashflows, NAV adjustments, and valuations matched within reporting tolerance, and documented any discrepancies in a structured mismatch report.

How It Is Used

The Datalake validation outputs help the data team catch and fix quality issues before they reach downstream reporting. The eFront UAT results directly inform the business decision on whether to switch to Front Cube as the primary server, given it is significantly faster but only refreshes overnight.

TSC & Proficiency Data Analytics L2 Data Engineering L3 Business Needs Analysis L2 Database Administration L3
Artefact 02 DealCloud Dashboard Design & Reporting Development

Description

A reporting dashboard built end-to-end in DealCloud to track task management, workload allocation, and hours spent across the team, starting as a sandbox prototype on a dummy dataset, then deployed to production once validated. DealCloud is the team's CRM and deal lifecycle platform, so the dashboard was designed around the Axiom Tasks object used by the Axiom MINDS data team to manage operational work such as updating fund, company, and contact information.

The dashboard provides a weekly snapshot of task progression by showing how many tasks were newly created, completed, or still open. It also breaks tasks down by assignee and includes hours spent, making workload easier to interpret because some tasks require significantly more effort than others. The KPI hours feature also supports pre-allocated hours with an overwrite option when actual effort is higher than expected.

My Contribution

I designed and built the entire dashboard myself: setting up the Axiom Minds objects, configuring the reporting structures, creating the KPI metrics and visualisations, and setting up all widgets and filters. It tracks task status trends over time, hours spent per team member by task type, weekly task status by assignee, and new tasks logged by date. I built a dummy dataset in the sandbox to test the layout, metric logic, filters, and widget behaviour before pushing to production, then supported the team during onboarding so the dashboard could be used consistently.

How It Is Used

Management and team leads use the dashboard to track open and completed tasks, monitor how hours are distributed, and get a clearer picture of weekly workload allocation, giving the team a live operational view to support resource planning and task prioritisation.

TSC & Proficiency Data Visualisation L2 Business Needs Analysis L2 Data Analytics L2 Stakeholder Management L3
Artefact 03 Public Markets Portfolio Tracking & Performance Reporting

Description

A recurring public markets portfolio tracker maintained in Excel, monitoring the organisation's public equity holdings across investment funds and co-investments. It consolidates share prices, currency conversions, holding valuations, realised proceeds, and gains and losses across multiple markets, including USD, HKD, JPY, TWD, and INR, refreshed weekly using Capital IQ integrations and formulas.

The Public Stock Tracker is an Excel template maintained for recurring stakeholder reporting. Each week, the reference date is updated, Capital IQ is used to refresh market prices, and investment-related values are checked against eFront records. The workbook includes summary and top-UPC views so stakeholders can quickly monitor the specific public companies and holdings that matter most to current discussions.

My Contribution

I was responsible for the weekly maintenance and update of the Public Stock Tracker workbook, refreshing market data through Capital IQ, validating ticker mappings and company identifiers, verifying share prices and currency conversions, and updating holding values, realised proceeds, and gains and losses. I also checked that the weekly reference date, Capital IQ formulas, and eFront-derived investment values aligned correctly across the summary and top-UPC tabs. When discrepancies came up, I investigated them, traced them back to the source, and resolved the issues to keep the portfolio information accurate and ready for distribution before the weekly reporting deadline.

How It Is Used

The tracker is used weekly by the investment team to monitor public equity portfolio performance across multiple funds and co-investments, feeding into internal portfolio reporting and supporting decisions around holdings and valuations.

TSC & Proficiency Data Analytics L2 Data Engineering L3 Business Performance Management L3 Database Administration L3

/ section 2 · generic skills & competencies

Competencies (CCS)

Task, actions taken, and results, for each core competency demonstrated during the internship.

CCS 01 Thinking Critically & Analytically

Task

During the Datalake validation work, I needed to verify that data flowing from eFront and DealCloud into the Computed Layer was accurate and consistent with the business rules in the source-to-target mapping document. This meant understanding the waterfall logic, checking field references, and identifying where transformation logic was not producing the expected outputs.

Actions Taken

The Databricks schema was unfamiliar at first and the waterfall logic wasn't immediately obvious. Rather than guessing, I worked through the mapping documents systematically, cross-referenced Raw and Computed Layer outputs column by column, and traced discrepancies back to their root cause. In some cases, the issue turned out to be in the mapping document itself rather than the data.

This required building enough finance and investment domain knowledge, such as how fund transactions are structured and how NAV adjustments and cashflows work, to judge whether a value looked right. When uncertain, I consulted colleagues rather than assuming, which helped me avoid misclassifying valid data as an error. I also had to learn how certain databases retain a full history of records rather than overwriting them, meaning the same entity could appear multiple times, so knowing when and how to deduplicate was essential to avoid double counting. For the eFront UAT, I applied the same structured approach to check whether numerical differences fell within acceptable tolerance or needed escalation.

Results

By working through the validation methodically and building the right domain context, I identified and documented data quality exceptions accurately, giving the team clear, actionable information. This demonstrated Level 2 proficiency: independently breaking down a complex problem, consulting others when needed, applying domain knowledge, and arriving at a well-reasoned conclusion.

CCS 02 Communicating & Relating

Task

Throughout the DealCloud dashboard development, I worked closely with my supervisor and team members to ensure the dashboard was being built in the right direction. This meant checking in regularly, walking them through progress, and incorporating feedback as the work progressed.

Actions Taken

As I built the dashboard, I periodically shared progress with my supervisor and got input on whether the layout, KPIs, and visualisations met the team's needs. Since I was working largely independently, these check-ins were important for staying on track. I listened carefully, asked clarifying questions, and made adjustments accordingly. In some cases, this meant reworking how metrics were calculated or displayed. I also communicated clearly whenever I hit uncertainty rather than making assumptions and building in the wrong direction.

Results

Regular communication meant the final dashboard came out aligned with what the team actually needed, and it's now used weekly for task and workload tracking. This demonstrated Level 2 competency: maintaining open communication, responding constructively to feedback, and knowing when to seek guidance rather than proceeding on assumptions alone.

CCS 03 Applying Technology Skills

Task

Across all three artefacts I had to pick up and apply tools and platforms I had little to no prior experience with: Databricks for data validation, DealCloud for dashboard development, and Capital IQ together with Excel for weekly portfolio tracking.

Actions Taken

For Databricks, I got up to speed on the data lake structure, how PySpark worked for querying and comparing large datasets, and how to navigate the Raw and Computed Layers. I did this by reading internal documentation, experimenting in the sandbox, and asking colleagues when stuck. For DealCloud, I learned how Axiom Minds objects and reporting structures worked by building the dashboard first in the sandbox with a dummy dataset before touching production. For Capital IQ, I learned how the formulas and data integrations worked within the existing Excel tracker and applied that consistently every week.

Results

I got productive with new tools relatively quickly by combining self-directed learning with hands-on practice and asking for help when needed. The DealCloud dashboard reaching production, and the weekly tracker running without reporting errors, are both concrete signs the technology was applied correctly. This demonstrated Level 2 proficiency: learning and using new platforms independently in a professional setting to deliver real business outcomes.

/ section 3 · student outlook & aspirations

Where I'm Headed

Nature of Work

A mix of BAU, validation, and self-owned builds

A large part of my regular work was business-as-usual: going through deal emails, fund update PDFs, and investor letters to extract information and keep DealCloud current. This meant tagging UPC records, refreshing fund and company-level data, updating contact information, and making sure investment records stayed accurate and usable for the team.

This day-to-day work required more than copying information across systems. I had to understand which details were relevant, identify whether an update affected a fund, company, contact, or deal record, and apply consistent naming and tagging practices so the CRM remained reliable for downstream searches and reporting.

Alongside that, I worked on data validation: checking that data flowing between eFront, DealCloud, and the Databricks data lake was accurate, working through mapping documents, running reconciliation checks, and documenting issues. I reviewed waterfall logic, calculated fields, business rules, and source-to-target mappings between the Raw and Computed Layers to confirm the data pipeline was behaving as intended.

The DealCloud dashboard was a more substantial piece of work I owned start to finish, from requirements and sandbox prototyping with dummy data through to production deployment and team onboarding. I configured the reporting objects, KPI metrics, visualisations, filters, and dashboard widgets used to track weekly task status, workload allocation, and hours spent by assignee.

Weekly, I also maintained the public markets portfolio tracker by refreshing Capital IQ data, checking ticker mappings, validating currency conversions, and preparing the workbook for distribution. Across all of this, the work involved both technical execution and judgment, not just running processes, but understanding what the data should look like and knowing when to flag something versus resolve it independently.

Challenges Faced

Building context before trusting the data

Getting up to speed with the Databricks data schema was one of the biggest early challenges. The structure across Raw and Computed Layers, and the business logic behind waterfall calculations, was something I had to piece together gradually before I could tell whether a value was correct or something had gone wrong upstream.

A related challenge was knowing when to trust the data versus question it. Some discrepancies were expected (like floating-point differences within tolerance), while others pointed to genuine mapping or logic issues. Telling the difference required both technical understanding and domain knowledge, and I learned to consult colleagues rather than assume, an adjustment from working independently. I also had to think carefully through deduplication logic in databases that retain full record history rather than overwriting.

On the dashboard side, the challenge was judging which of many possible widgets and views were genuinely useful versus clutter, which required back-and-forth with my supervisor and staying focused on what the team would actually use regularly. I had to balance visual detail with readability, especially for task status trends, hours spent, and assignee-level workload views.

Learning & Growth

From no experience to production-ready outputs

Coming in as a Year 3 student, I expected fairly surface-level work, but ended up involved in things with real consequences for financial reporting accuracy, which raised the bar for how carefully I approached everything.

Technically, I went from no experience with Databricks, DealCloud, or Capital IQ to using all three productively in a professional setting. I learned to query and compare datasets in Databricks, configure reporting in DealCloud, and use Capital IQ integrations in Excel for time-sensitive market updates.

More importantly, I learned how to learn new tools quickly without a structured onboarding, through documentation, experimentation, sandbox testing, and asking the right people the right questions. That experience made me more confident working with unfamiliar platforms and more comfortable taking ownership of work where the full solution was not obvious at the beginning.

I also developed a much stronger practical sense of data quality: the difference between understanding validation as a concept and being responsible for catching issues before they reach fund managers and investors. Beyond the technical, I grew in how I communicate within a team: checking in at the right moments, framing questions clearly, taking feedback without getting defensive, and getting comfortable navigating ambiguity.

Experiences

Exposure to cloud, AI, and deal technology trends

I attended an AWS event at Marina Bay Sands that focused on how AI is changing cloud-based data infrastructure. The sessions helped me connect my data lake work to a broader architecture: storage through services such as S3, ingestion through crawlers, and automated ETL or workflow processes through services such as AWS Lambda. Seeing how these components support unified repositories and advanced analytics gave me a clearer understanding of why strong data foundations matter beyond the immediate project.

The event also introduced newer AI capabilities such as Bedrock, which provides access to large language models through a unified API, and AWS Connect use cases involving agentic AI for areas like customer service, supply chain planning, hiring solutions, and healthcare workflows. Hearing sector specialists explain how they scaled AWS-based systems and overcame implementation roadblocks gave me a wider view of how AI and cloud computing are being adopted outside the technology sector, including in finance.

I also attended an Intapp webinar on Celeste, a firm-focused AI designed to help organisations use proprietary DealCloud data securely. This was especially relevant to private equity because proprietary relationship and deal data can be a competitive advantage. The webinar showed how AI could help investment teams query internal data, map customer and team relationships, compare deals by sector or geography, and streamline decision-making while protecting sensitive information.
